chapterTitle: Planning and Pre-migration Assessment for Azure Database Migrations

Create a 12-minute video tutorial demonstrating a pre-migration assessment. Start by showing the download and installation of Data Migration Assistant (DMA). Then, walk through connecting DMA to a local SQL Server instance (e.g., `AdventureWorks2019`), selecting "Azure SQL Database" as the target, and running an assessment. Visually highlight and explain the "Compatibility issues" and "Feature parity" tabs in the DMA report, focusing on a few common "Breaking changes" (like CLR assemblies) and "Behavior changes." End with a reflection prompt asking users to consider a specific breaking change and how they would refactor their code.

screens.title: Planning and Pre-migration Assessment
screens.narratorSegment: Migrating databases to Azure starts long before data transfer begins. In this lesson you will learn how structured planning and a careful pre-migration assessment reduce risks, limit downtime, and control cost. Assessment tools such as the Data Migration Assistant focus on database compatibility, while Azure Migrate provides a broader discovery and rightsizing view across servers. Together they reveal breaking changes, behavior changes, unsupported features, and resource sizing needs. For example, DMA will flag CLR assemblies or unsupported data types that must be refactored; Azure Migrate will show historic C P U and memory trends that inform the correct Azure SKU. We will also discuss migration strategies — online methods that keep the source active during replication, offline approaches for simpler moves, and hybrid patterns for phased cutover. A common mistake is treating assessment as optional and discovering blockers only during migration; instead, treat assessment as the primary planning activity. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to run an assessment, interpret reports, choose an appropriate Azure target, and draft a migration approach that matches your application's downtime and testing constraints.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will gain practical skills for planning and assessing database migrations to Azure. First, you'll learn to identify key migration phases and critical considerations that shape a migration plan. This covers discovery, assessment, remediation, and cutover, and why each matters for uptime and cost. Second, you'll learn to use Data Migration Assistant to assess S Q L Server databases for compatibility issues and feature parity; you'll see how DMA flags breaking and behavior changes and what each finding implies. Third, you'll use Azure Migrate to discover servers and perform rightsizing based on historical performance data so you can select the appropriate Azure SKU without over-provisioning. Fourth, you'll practice choosing and justifying migration strategies — online, offline, and hybrid — aligned to application downtime tolerance and complexity. Each objective includes a verification milestone so you know when you've reached competency: running DMA, interpreting its report, performing a discovery with Azure Migrate, and drafting a migration plan with a chosen strategy.

screens.title: Pre-migration Assessment: Purpose and Scope
screens.narratorSegment: A pre-migration assessment is the structured process of discovering your database estate, evaluating compatibility and performance, and drafting a migration plan. Think of it as a health check and planning exercise combined. Discovery inventories servers, databases, and dependent applications so you understand scope. Assessment evaluates schema, server-level objects, and application calls to find compatibility gaps and performance constraints. Planning then converts those findings into remediation tasks, a migration strategy, and a testing schedule. A concrete example: you discover an on-premises S Q L Server hosting several databases, and the assessment flags CLR assemblies and S Q L Agent jobs. The planning step decides which databases require refactoring, which jobs should move to Azure Automation or Elastic Jobs, and whether Managed Instance or S Q L VM is the target. A common misconception is assuming assessment is optional for small databases. Even small systems can have hidden dependencies or deprecated features; skipping assessment often causes unexpected downtime. Key takeaway: assessment reduces uncertainty by turning unknowns into a prioritized checklist of work and helps you select the migration approach that matches your application's uptime and testing needs.

screens.title: Data Migration Assistant (DMA)
screens.narratorSegment: The Data Migration Assistant is a targeted assessment tool for S Q L Server databases that evaluates schema, server-level objects, and application compatibility for Azure targets. DMA flags three major classes of findings: breaking changes that will prevent functionality, behavior changes that alter semantics without necessarily breaking, and feature parity gaps where an exact match is not available. A practical example: DMA may flag a CLR assembly as a breaking change for Azure S Q L Database, because the platform doesn't support CLR. In that case, the remediation options are refactor to T-S Q L, move logic out to the app or an Azure Function, or pick Managed Instance or a S Q L VM that supports CLR. DMA produces exportable reports that list issues, affected objects, and recommended actions; these reports become the input to your migration backlog. A common misconception is treating DMA as only a checklist of fixes; instead, use DMA output to estimate effort and to decide on the target service. Key takeaway: DMA translates technical compatibility into prioritized remediation steps and informs whether refactoring or a different Azure target is the more appropriate path.

screens.title: Azure Migrate vs DMA
screens.narratorSegment: Azure Migrate and Data Migration Assistant are complementary. DMA specializes in database-level compatibility and feature-parity analysis for S Q L Server. It inspects schema, CLR usage, server-level objects, and application calls that reference database objects. Azure Migrate provides estate-level discovery: it finds servers, maps dependencies between applications and servers, and analyzes historical performance so you can rightsizing appropriately. Use DMA when your focus is a single database or set of databases and you need explicit compatibility findings. Use Azure Migrate when you need a holistic view across many servers, to understand application dependencies, or to produce rightsizing recommendations for SKU selection. A practical scenario: use Azure Migrate to discover an environment and build a list of S Q L Server instances; then run DMA on each critical database to capture breaking changes and remediation tasks. A common misconception is that DMA replaces Azure Migrate—this is not true. DMA does not provide rightsizing nor cross-server dependency mapping. Key takeaway: combine Azure Migrate for scope and sizing with DMA for deep compatibility analysis to form a complete migration plan. Azure Migrate vs DMA means azure migrate for discovery and sizing; dma for database compatibility and remediation guidance.. In practical terms, when to use each tool and how they complement each other. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Analyzing DMA Reports
screens.narratorSegment: Interpreting DMA output correctly is essential to create a realistic remediation plan. Start by identifying breaking changes because they will prevent your database or application from functioning in the target environment until fixed. Examples include unsupported CLR assemblies or server-level objects that do not exist in a PaaS offering. Next, review behavior changes — these may not immediately break your system but can alter results or performance; these require targeted testing. Feature parity items are next: where the target provides similar but not identical functionality, plan compensating changes or accept reasonable substitutes. For each finding, estimate effort: small fixes like changing a data type might be quick, while refactoring CLR logic could be a larger work item that may push you toward another target. Use DMA reports to build a prioritized backlog, estimate remediation timelines, and inform your migration approach. A misconception to avoid is treating all DMA findings as equal; prioritize by impact and frequency of use. Key takeaway: use DMA to turn technical findings into prioritized, time-boxed tasks that feed into your migration schedule and cutover plan. Analyzing DMA Reports means breakers first, then behavior changes, then feature parity. estimate effort and schedule remediation accordingly.. In practical terms, how to prioritize breaking changes, behavior changes, and remediation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Report Analysis Workflow
Identify impact, estimate effort, and prioritize remediation.
Breaking Changes

Behavior Changes

Feature Parity

screens.title: Choosing the Right Azure Target
screens.narratorSegment: Selecting the appropriate Azure target is a central outcome of assessment. Azure S Q L Database is a fully managed PaaS ideal for modern cloud apps without server-level dependencies and where platform-managed updates are acceptable. Azure S Q L Managed Instance offers broader S Q L Server compatibility, making it a good choice when server-level features matter but you still want PaaS benefits. S Q L Server on Azure Virtual Machines gives the most compatibility and control because it's essentially a lift-and-shift of your S Q L Server instance into Azure; use this when you cannot refactor features or when you rely on unsupported server components. A concrete example: if DMA flags CLR assemblies and refactoring is impractical, Managed Instance or S Q L VM could be chosen — Managed Instance if most other features are compatible, S Q L VM if operating-system-level control is required. A common misconception is that PaaS is always cheaper; cost depends on rightsizing and operational choices. Key takeaway: let compatibility findings and remediation effort drive the target choice, and verify with Azure Migrate sizing data to avoid over- or under-provisioning.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Choosing the Right Target
Target Options
Match compatibility needs with operational objectives.
Azure SQL Database (PaaS)
Best for modern cloud apps without server-level dependencies; highest managed service benefits.
Azure SQL Managed Instance
Offers broad compatibility while providing many PaaS benefits for easier migrations from on-premises.
SQL Server on VM
Lift-and-shift option for maximum compatibility and OS-level control at the cost of managed features.
Decision Example
DMA flags CLR assemblies and linked servers; Azure Migrate shows steady CPU and memory underutilization.
Option 1
Refactor CLR to T-SQL and move to Azure SQL Database — lowest operational overhead but requires code change.
Option 2
Choose Managed Instance to preserve compatibility with minimal refactor if other server features are used.
Key Takeaway

Compatibility findings and remediation effort should drive whether you accept PaaS or choose a more compatible hosting option.

screens.title: Migration Strategies: Online, Offline, Hybrid
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing a migration strategy balances downtime tolerance, data volume, and schema complexity. Offline migration is straightforward: take the source offline, copy data using backup/restore or export/import, and bring up the target. It is suitable when brief downtime is acceptable or for non-production environments. Online migration aims to minimize downtime by continuously synchronizing changes from source to target until cutover; services like Azure Database Migration Service often support continuous replication for S Q L Server. Hybrid approaches combine bulk transfer with a short final synchronization window, useful for very large datasets where a pure online sync would take too long to seed. A concrete example: for a mission-critical transactional system with low downtime tolerance, use Azure DMS continuous replication to seed the target, validate data, and perform a brief cutover. A common misconception is assuming online migration eliminates the need for testing — it does not. You still need end-to-end tests and verification, and you must plan rollback steps. Key takeaway: pick the strategy that matches downtime SLAs and testing capacity, and always include a rollback plan and sufficient testing time in the schedule.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Migration Strategies
Offline Migration
Backup/restore or export/import requiring downtime. Useful for test/dev or low-impact apps.
Online Migration
Continuous synchronization to minimize downtime, typically using DMS for cutover-ready replication.
Hybrid Migration
Seed data using a bulk method, then use replication for final delta to shorten cutover windows.
Example
Use DMS continuous replication for mission-critical systems and schedule a short cutover once sync is complete.
Common Mistake
Assuming online migration eliminates the need for end-to-end testing or rollback planning.
Key Takeaway

Strategy choice depends on downtime tolerance, size, and test readiness. Always include rollback and test windows.

screens.title: Rightsizing with Azure Migrate
screens.narratorSegment: Rightsizing is the process of selecting an appropriate Azure SKU that meets your workload's performance and capacity needs without over-provisioning. Azure Migrate examines historical C P U, memory, and input and output metrics to recommend SKUs for Azure S Q L Database, Managed Instance, or VMs. The assessment helps avoid two frequent problems: undersizing, which causes performance problems after migration, and oversizing, which wastes cost. A practical example: Azure Migrate shows consistent 30% C P U and 40% memory usage on average, with occasional spikes that require a higher burst capacity. The recommended SKU should handle peaks and sustained usage; you might choose a tier with higher IOPS or enable scaling. A common misconception is trusting a single short monitoring window; you need representative historical data covering peak and low usage cycles. Key takeaway: use Azure Migrate's rightsizing as a baseline, then validate with load tests and include vertical or horizontal scaling options in your migration runbook. Rightsizing with Azure Migrate means use historical metrics for sku selection, validate with load tests, and plan scaling to handle peak loads.. In practical terms, using historical metrics to choose an appropriate sku. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Testing, Backup, and Rollback Planning
screens.narratorSegment: Testing and rollback planning are essential safety nets for any migration. Always take a full backup before migration steps and verify that backups are restorable. screens.title: Operational Considerations: Network, Security, and Bandwidth
screens.narratorSegment: Network, security, and bandwidth are operational constraints that affect migration feasibility and speed. Verify that the machine running DMA or DMS has network access to the source S Q L Server and to Azure endpoints. For large datasets, limited bandwidth can make initial seeding slow; consider a bulk transfer followed by delta sync or use an accelerated transfer option when available. Security is also critical: ensure authentication types, firewall rules, and encryption settings are configured so assessment tools can connect securely. fullNarratorScript:
Migrating databases to Azure starts long before data transfer begins. In this lesson you will learn how structured planning and a careful pre-migration assessment reduce risks, limit downtime, and control cost. Assessment tools such as the Data Migration Assistant focus on database compatibility, while Azure Migrate provides a broader discovery and rightsizing view across servers. Together they reveal breaking changes, behavior changes, unsupported features, and resource sizing needs. For example, DMA will flag CLR assemblies or unsupported data types that must be refactored; Azure Migrate will show historic C P U and memory trends that inform the correct Azure SKU. We will also discuss migration strategies — online methods that keep the source active during replication, offline approaches for simpler moves, and hybrid patterns for phased cutover. A common mistake is treating assessment as optional and discovering blockers only during migration; instead, treat assessment as the primary planning activity. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to run an assessment, interpret reports, choose an appropriate Azure target, and draft a migration approach that matches your application's downtime and testing constraints.

In this chapter you will gain practical skills for planning and assessing database migrations to Azure. First, you'll learn to identify key migration phases and critical considerations that shape a migration plan. This covers discovery, assessment, remediation, and cutover, and why each matters for uptime and cost. Second, you'll learn to use Data Migration Assistant to assess S Q L Server databases for compatibility issues and feature parity; you'll see how DMA flags breaking and behavior changes and what each finding implies. Third, you'll use Azure Migrate to discover servers and perform rightsizing based on historical performance data so you can select the appropriate Azure SKU without over-provisioning. Fourth, you'll practice choosing and justifying migration strategies — online, offline, and hybrid — aligned to application downtime tolerance and complexity. Each objective includes a verification milestone so you know when you've reached competency: running DMA, interpreting its report, performing a discovery with Azure Migrate, and drafting a migration plan with a chosen strategy.

This second objectives slide focuses on tools, what they produce, and the concrete actions you will take from their output. The Data Migration Assistant produces database-level compatibility checks, breaking-change listings, and feature parity recommendations. You will learn how to interpret each finding and map it to remediation choices: refactor code, move logic to the app layer, or choose a different Azure service. Azure Migrate, by contrast, provides server discovery, dependency mapping, and rightsizing recommendations based on past performance. You will practice taking Azure Migrate output and converting it to an Azure SKU selection for Azure S Q L Database or Managed Instance. Importantly, you will also learn how to combine these outputs: compatibility issues drive remediation effort and target selection, while rightsizing ensures cost-effective capacity planning. The verified milestone for these objectives is a combined assessment sheet that lists compatibility blockers, estimated refactor effort, chosen Azure target, and a recommended migration approach.

A pre-migration assessment is the structured process of discovering your database estate, evaluating compatibility and performance, and drafting a migration plan. Think of it as a health check and planning exercise combined. Discovery inventories servers, databases, and dependent applications so you understand scope. Assessment evaluates schema, server-level objects, and application calls to find compatibility gaps and performance constraints. Planning then converts those findings into remediation tasks, a migration strategy, and a testing schedule. A concrete example: you discover an on-premises S Q L Server hosting several databases, and the assessment flags CLR assemblies and S Q L Agent jobs. The planning step decides which databases require refactoring, which jobs should move to Azure Automation or Elastic Jobs, and whether Managed Instance or S Q L VM is the target. A common misconception is assuming assessment is optional for small databases. Even small systems can have hidden dependencies or deprecated features; skipping assessment often causes unexpected downtime. Key takeaway: assessment reduces uncertainty by turning unknowns into a prioritized checklist of work and helps you select the migration approach that matches your application's uptime and testing needs.

The Data Migration Assistant is a targeted assessment tool for S Q L Server databases that evaluates schema, server-level objects, and application compatibility for Azure targets. DMA flags three major classes of findings: breaking changes that will prevent functionality, behavior changes that alter semantics without necessarily breaking, and feature parity gaps where an exact match is not available. A practical example: DMA may flag a CLR assembly as a breaking change for Azure S Q L Database, because the platform doesn't support CLR. In that case, the remediation options are refactor to T-S Q L, move logic out to the app or an Azure Function, or pick Managed Instance or a S Q L VM that supports CLR. DMA produces exportable reports that list issues, affected objects, and recommended actions; these reports become the input to your migration backlog. A common misconception is treating DMA as only a checklist of fixes; instead, use DMA output to estimate effort and to decide on the target service. Key takeaway: DMA translates technical compatibility into prioritized remediation steps and informs whether refactoring or a different Azure target is the more appropriate path.

Azure Migrate and Data Migration Assistant are complementary. DMA specializes in database-level compatibility and feature-parity analysis for S Q L Server. It inspects schema, CLR usage, server-level objects, and application calls that reference database objects. Azure Migrate provides estate-level discovery: it finds servers, maps dependencies between applications and servers, and analyzes historical performance so you can rightsizing appropriately. Use DMA when your focus is a single database or set of databases and you need explicit compatibility findings. Use Azure Migrate when you need a holistic view across many servers, to understand application dependencies, or to produce rightsizing recommendations for SKU selection. A practical scenario: use Azure Migrate to discover an environment and build a list of S Q L Server instances; then run DMA on each critical database to capture breaking changes and remediation tasks. A common misconception is that DMA replaces Azure Migrate—this is not true. DMA does not provide rightsizing nor cross-server dependency mapping. Key takeaway: combine Azure Migrate for scope and sizing with DMA for deep compatibility analysis to form a complete migration plan. Azure Migrate vs DMA means azure migrate for discovery and sizing; dma for database compatibility and remediation guidance.. In practical terms, when to use each tool and how they complement each other. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Interpreting DMA output correctly is essential to create a realistic remediation plan. Start by identifying breaking changes because they will prevent your database or application from functioning in the target environment until fixed. Examples include unsupported CLR assemblies or server-level objects that do not exist in a PaaS offering. Next, review behavior changes — these may not immediately break your system but can alter results or performance; these require targeted testing. Feature parity items are next: where the target provides similar but not identical functionality, plan compensating changes or accept reasonable substitutes. For each finding, estimate effort: small fixes like changing a data type might be quick, while refactoring CLR logic could be a larger work item that may push you toward another target. Use DMA reports to build a prioritized backlog, estimate remediation timelines, and inform your migration approach. A misconception to avoid is treating all DMA findings as equal; prioritize by impact and frequency of use. Key takeaway: use DMA to turn technical findings into prioritized, time-boxed tasks that feed into your migration schedule and cutover plan. Analyzing DMA Reports means breakers first, then behavior changes, then feature parity. estimate effort and schedule remediation accordingly.. In practical terms, how to prioritize breaking changes, behavior changes, and remediation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Selecting the appropriate Azure target is a central outcome of assessment. Azure S Q L Database is a fully managed PaaS ideal for modern cloud apps without server-level dependencies and where platform-managed updates are acceptable. Azure S Q L Managed Instance offers broader S Q L Server compatibility, making it a good choice when server-level features matter but you still want PaaS benefits. S Q L Server on Azure Virtual Machines gives the most compatibility and control because it's essentially a lift-and-shift of your S Q L Server instance into Azure; use this when you cannot refactor features or when you rely on unsupported server components. A concrete example: if DMA flags CLR assemblies and refactoring is impractical, Managed Instance or S Q L VM could be chosen — Managed Instance if most other features are compatible, S Q L VM if operating-system-level control is required. A common misconception is that PaaS is always cheaper; cost depends on rightsizing and operational choices. Key takeaway: let compatibility findings and remediation effort drive the target choice, and verify with Azure Migrate sizing data to avoid over- or under-provisioning.

Choosing a migration strategy balances downtime tolerance, data volume, and schema complexity. Offline migration is straightforward: take the source offline, copy data using backup/restore or export/import, and bring up the target. It is suitable when brief downtime is acceptable or for non-production environments. Online migration aims to minimize downtime by continuously synchronizing changes from source to target until cutover; services like Azure Database Migration Service often support continuous replication for S Q L Server. Hybrid approaches combine bulk transfer with a short final synchronization window, useful for very large datasets where a pure online sync would take too long to seed. A concrete example: for a mission-critical transactional system with low downtime tolerance, use Azure DMS continuous replication to seed the target, validate data, and perform a brief cutover. A common misconception is assuming online migration eliminates the need for testing — it does not. You still need end-to-end tests and verification, and you must plan rollback steps. Key takeaway: pick the strategy that matches downtime SLAs and testing capacity, and always include a rollback plan and sufficient testing time in the schedule.

Rightsizing is the process of selecting an appropriate Azure SKU that meets your workload's performance and capacity needs without over-provisioning. Azure Migrate examines historical C P U, memory, and input and output metrics to recommend SKUs for Azure S Q L Database, Managed Instance, or VMs. The assessment helps avoid two frequent problems: undersizing, which causes performance problems after migration, and oversizing, which wastes cost. A practical example: Azure Migrate shows consistent 30% C P U and 40% memory usage on average, with occasional spikes that require a higher burst capacity. The recommended SKU should handle peaks and sustained usage; you might choose a tier with higher IOPS or enable scaling. A common misconception is trusting a single short monitoring window; you need representative historical data covering peak and low usage cycles. Key takeaway: use Azure Migrate's rightsizing as a baseline, then validate with load tests and include vertical or horizontal scaling options in your migration runbook.
